newsitem.title: GERMANY: Ex-Chancellor Schmidt raps German line on Europe.
newsitem.headline: Ex-Chancellor Schmidt raps German line on Europe.

text.p: Former German Chancellor Helmut Schmidt said on Tuesday Bonn's tough line on monetary union was wrecking Franco-German relations.

Schmidt said Germany failed at last week's European Union summit in its bid for a tough stability pact with compulsory fines for states which overborrow, while France made sure the political discretion enshrined in the Maastricht treaty stayed.

With his successor Helmut Kohl and French President Jacques Chirac unable to agree a common position ahead of the summit "we are as far from a Bonn-Paris axis as we have been in decades," Schmidt wrote in the Die Zeit weekly newspaper.
Schmidt, Germany's Social Democratic Chancellor from 1974 to 1982, uses the pages of Die Zeit, which he co-publishes, to launch regular blasts against Kohl and his lieutenants.

After rapping Finance Minister Theo Waigel and Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer last month, this time he accused German leaders of "know-it-all" dogmatism which could ultimately prove counterproductive.
"Without France close by our sides, Germany could quickly become isolated," Schmidt said, harking back to bitter memories there of Germany's wartime occupation of its neighbour.
"Kohl must watch out that neither his Finance Minister nor the Bundesbank, nor the Foreign Minister and his bureaucrats don't break too much china in relations with France," he added.

German leaders hailed the result of the Dublin summit as a sound compromise but Bundesbank chief economist Otmar Issing on Tuesday attacked the stability pact for lacking "automaticity" and giving governments political licence to overspend.
Schmidt's tone reflects that of his French contemporary Valery Giscard d'Estaing, who has won support from some quarters for a weaker franc to boost growth and beat unemployment.
But Schmidt, 77, is very much a lone voice in Germany, and is seen by many to be still settling old scores dating back to his toppling from power in 1982.
He also said that France and Germany were both on the wrong track, with overvalued currencies and misplaced policies.
"Neither country is in particularly good shape socially or economically, the franc and the mark are overvalued, and the "German model" no longer exists," he wrote.
